title: Functional interpretation of GWAS · Thursday, November 26

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Functional interpretation of GWAS, for Thursday, November 26.
Let's turn to Functional interpretation of GWAS, where several new papers ask how risk variants reach genes and cell states.
First, a medRxiv preprint from the Dyke lab asks whether the heritability of gene expression in single cells shifts with cell state.

Their method, scHINT, splits expression heritability into a main genetic part and a genotype by cell-state part. In brain single-nucleus data, the cell-state part was common and on average larger than the main part. It was also concentrated in constrained genes and disease heritability.
In a cell-state-aware TWAS, it found sixty-eight percent more disease risk genes than a standard TWAS, including TREM2. It's still a preprint, and it uses brain data only.

The Wang lab, in Advanced Science, extends TWAS differently. Their method, GRNTWAS, adds trans variants chosen through gene regulatory networks. It predicted expression better and prioritized well-supported genes across twelve neuropsychiatric traits.

Next, a bioRxiv preprint from the Lee lab links enhancers to target genes within each cell type. Their method, CREMAP, learns shared technical and biological variation from single-cell multiome data and removes it before testing each peak-gene pair.
The idea is that adjusting for sample covariates can also remove real genetic effects. On CRISPRi and fine-mapped eQTL benchmarks, it beat existing methods in two cell lines and thirteen cell types.

Third, a bioRxiv preprint from the Lettre lab used a pangenome reference to genotype about six hundred forty-six thousand structural variants in two thousand one hundred seventy-three CARTaGENE participants.

Conditioning on known small variants, they found ninety-nine structural variant eQTLs, and forty-one replicated in the thousand Genomes data. Two thirds are in strong LD with Open Targets credible sets, making them candidate causal variants, though LD alone can't prove causality.

Finally, a bioRxiv preprint from the Pang lab studied an alcohol use disorder locus in microglia. Knocking out or editing the variant rs7307261 in iPSC-derived microglia stopped ethanol from inducing CD163 and changed phagocytosis.
The takeaway is that interpreting GWAS increasingly means modelling cell context, from cell state down to enhancer-gene links within each cell type, rather than averaging it away.
